abstracts.value: Precision measurements by the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer (AMS) on the International Space Station of the deuteron (<math display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>) flux are presented. The measurements are based on <math display="inline"><mrow><mn>21</mn><mo>×</mo><msup><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> <math display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> nuclei in the rigidity range from 1.9 to 21 GV collected from May 2011 to April 2021. We observe that over the entire rigidity range the <math display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> flux exhibits nearly identical time variations with the <math display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>, <math display="inline"><mrow><mmultiscripts><mrow><mi>He</mi></mrow><mprescripts/><none/><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mmultiscripts></mrow></math>, and <math display="inline"><mrow><mmultiscripts><mrow><mi>He</mi></mrow><mprescripts/><none/><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mmultiscripts></mrow></math> fluxes. Above 4.5 GV, the <math display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mmultiscripts><mrow><mi>He</mi></mrow><mprescripts/><none/><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mmultiscripts></mrow></mrow></math> flux ratio is time independent and its rigidity dependence is well described by a single power law <math display="inline"><mrow><mo>∝</mo><msup><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> with <math display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mmultiscripts><mrow><mi>He</mi></mrow><mprescripts/><none/><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mmultiscripts></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>-</mo><mn>0.108</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>0.005</mn></mrow></math>. This is in contrast with the <math display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mmultiscripts><mrow><mi>He</mi></mrow><mprescripts/><none/><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mmultiscripts></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mmultiscripts><mrow><mi>He</mi></mrow><mprescripts/><none/><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mmultiscripts></mrow></mrow></math> flux ratio for which we find <math display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mmultiscripts><mrow><mi>He</mi></mrow><mprescripts/><none/><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mmultiscripts></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mmultiscripts><mrow><mi>He</mi></mrow><mprescripts/><none/><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mmultiscripts></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>-</mo><mn>0.289</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>0.003</mn></mrow></math>. Above <math display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">∼</mo><mn>13</mn><mtext> </mtext><mtext> </mtext><mi>GV</mi></mrow></math> we find a nearly identical rigidity dependence of the <math display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> and <math display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> fluxes with a <math display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> flux ratio of <math display="inline"><mn>0.027</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>0.001</mn></math>. These unexpected observations indicate that cosmic deuterons have a sizable primarylike component. With a method independent of cosmic ray propagation, we obtain the primary component of the <math display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> flux equal to <math display="inline"><mn>9.4</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo>%</mo></math> of the <math display="inline"><mrow><mmultiscripts><mrow><mi>He</mi></mrow><mprescripts/><none/><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mmultiscripts></mrow></math> flux and the secondary component of the <math display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> flux equal to <math display="inline"><mn>58</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></math> of the <math display="inline"><mrow><mmultiscripts><mrow><mi>He</mi></mrow><mprescripts/><none/><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mmultiscripts></mrow></math> flux.
